script.title: Why the Radium Girls Licked Poison

lines: A young woman licked a brush dipped in glowing paint.
She painted up to 250 dials a shift.
From 1917, in Orange, New Jersey, young women painted watch faces that glowed in the dark.
They earned about a penny and a half per dial.
The tiny brushes kept losing their point.
So supervisors told them: lip, dip, paint.
The women were told the paint was harmless.
Some even painted their nails and teeth with it, for fun.
Meanwhile, the company's chemists handled radium with lead screens, tongs and masks.
Then the painters' teeth came loose.
Their bones broke. Their jaws rotted.
In 1923, one painter's jaw fell away before she died.
The glow came from radium, a radioactive material.
Every lick put a little inside their bodies.
You see, it's like a dripping tap filling a bucket.
One drop is nothing. Thousands flood the floor.
The company blamed the deaths on other causes.
By 1927, more than 50 of the painters had died.
The women's lawsuits changed safety laws for workers.
And the man who invented the glowing paint died from it too.

claims.claim: The women pointed their brushes on their lips; the paint was self-luminous radium paint used on watch dials.
Around 1917 the factory in Orange, New Jersey, employed women to paint radium-lit watch faces.
The pay was about a penny and a half per dial.
The brushes lost shape, so supervisors encouraged workers to shape the point with their lips ('lip, dip, paint').
The women were told the paint was harmless; some painted their nails and teeth for fun.
Chemists at the plant used lead screens, tongs and masks.
Workers had loose teeth, bone fractures and necrosis of the jaw; in 1923 the first dial painter died after her jaw fell away.
The paint was made from powdered radium; radium-contaminated dust was radioactive material; the women ingested radium.
At the company's urging, medical professionals attributed worker deaths to other causes.
By 1927 more than 50 of the female factory workers had died from radium poisoning.
Lawsuits by the women had lasting effects on labor laws; the inventor of radium dial paint died in 1928 of radium poisoning.
